answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Using consequential accounting methods for electricity-sector actions offers transformative benefits for driving real climate impact. Consequential methods measure the actual emissions changes that result from procurement decisions, ensuring that reported reductions reflect genuine climate progress rather than accounting artifacts or geographic/time-based proxies. By focusing on real system-level emissions effects, consequential accounting directly aligns corporate action with the fundamental goal of accelerating global decarbonization. Evidence underscores this: ZEROgrid (Steinsultz 2025) demonstrates that procurement in high-emissions grids—where marginal generators are dirtier—has substantially greater carbon impact than procurement optimized for hourly matching alone.

A focus on carbon impact also addresses a major equity concern: the geographic imbalance in clean energy investment. Baringa (“The Corporate Catalyst”) finds that nearly 80% of corporate PPAs in 2023 were signed in Europe and the Americas, driven in part by requirements to procure within the same market boundaries as a company’s load. Such constraints concentrate investment in grids already progressing toward decarbonization while leaving behind regions where added clean energy would deliver significantly greater climate value. A consequential metric—incentivizing procurement where emissions benefits are greatest, regardless of time or location—would promote a more equitable global distribution of clean energy investment. This ensures that grids and communities in the Global South are less likely to be left behind in the clean energy transition.

Organizations are already demonstrating this approach by procuring clean energy in dirtier grid regions that avoid more emissions where they may not have substantial load. For example, Boston University procured a wind project in North Dakota, Salesforce procured clean energy in emerging markets, and California uses consequential methods to determine the emissions impact of energy storage receiving a SGIP incentive.

This approach is also highly feasible, as it leverages marginal emissions data that is academically verified, widely published, and increasingly accessible—often at minimal or no cost. The data has also been integrated in simple, accessible calculators. Because this framework builds on existing data infrastructure, research indicates that implementation costs would not substantially increase compared to current methods (Steinsultz 2025), preserving broad participation by organizations of all sizes.

Crucially, a strict additionality requirement must be included within a consequential framework as it ensures that the proposed method drives new renewable capacity rather than merely reallocating claims to existing clean energy. This safeguards against reporting gimmicks and is essential for ensuring that procurement decisions translate into real-world atmospheric benefit.

Finally, while many organizations already deploy this approach as part of their clean energy procurement strategies, there is no clear guidance on how to integrate it into target setting and reporting.

As an organization with strong commitments to global climate equity, we view these benefits as integral. For these reasons, we strongly believe that the GHG Protocol should adopt a required consequential metric- with induced emissions, avoided emissions, and robust additionality requirements- into the Corporate Standard Scope 2 Guidance.

Resources:
ZEROgrid, Steinsultz 2025: https://zerogrid.org/wp-content/uploads/dlm_uploads/2025/05/iai-review-research-voluntary-energy-procurement.pdf
Baringa, “The Corporate Catalyst” 2024: https://www.baringa.com/en/insights/low-carbon-capital/the-corporate-catalyst/
Steinsultz 2025: “Evaluating the Impacts, Costs, and Consequences of Proposed Scope 2 GHG Emissions Reporting Standards”: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5375940

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
The equation presented in this consultation is insufficient for quantifying the emissions impacts of organizations because it omits a key component: induced emissions. The proposed formula represents only one part of a decision-useful consequential framework. A full consequential metric, such as the one developed and sent to the ISB by the Consequential Subgroup (“Public Letter…”), includes both induced and avoided emissions. The induced emissions calculation creates a baseline to which the avoided emissions can be compared. Without it, the current framework asks reporting entities to perform calculations that do not inform procurement decisions or target-setting. The proposed formula quantifies impacts without providing the tools to contextualize those quantifications and enable action. Without these elements that enable an organization to show how its interventions have made progress towards emissions targets, it is unlikely that this metric will be adopted and used by reporting organizations.

Project accounting already exists in the Project Protocol. Part of the reason organizations don’t use the Project Protocol is that it only reflects the reductions achieved and is not recognized in their inventory reporting or goals and target setting. goals. For years, we’ve heard companies ask us whether they can use their Scope 2 inventory emissions and subtract the avoided emissions from projects to track their progress toward their climate goals. This is not a valid way to assess progress, since it mixes attributional and consequential frameworks. It also confuses these companies as they wonder why they can’t account for the results of their actions in their inventory.

A complete equation would allow companies to evaluate the net effects of procurement choices and make strategic decisions accordingly. As currently structured, the formula lacks decision-making value and would perpetuate the already existing confusion and urge to mix consequential impact with attributional baselines. A full formulation that enables actionable target setting is essential, rather than an accounting exercise disconnected from organizational priorities and target-setting practices.

Resources:
Public Statement from Members of the GHG Protocol Scope 2 TWG Consequential Subgroup: https://marginalimpactmethod.org/

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text:
Whether projects should be assessed for the reporting year or the lifetime of the project depends on the metric’s use case. When used as a planning and decision tool, the impact of a project should be projected over its lifetime to estimate the potential impact of investing in it.

Conversely, when determining the realized impacts of a project, the impacts should be reported each year using historical emissions data instead of forecasted data. The realized impacts based on historical data should be used to assess progress against climate goals and targets, as projected data is inappropriate for this since real conditions may change.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
In alignment with the research from Brander (2025) and as proposed by the consequential sub-group (“Public Statement…”), a set of consequential tests should be implemented in combination.

A timing test ensures that the procuring organization’s investment actually occurs before the decision to proceed with the project. Failing a timing test indicates that the organization’s investment was unnecessary to construct the project and therefore an organization should not receive credit.
Similarly, if a project is required by regulation and not chosen by the organization, the organization should not receive credit.

Finally, a financing test which shows that the organization materially contributed to the financing of the project through either revenue guarantees/offtake agreements or other mechanism is essential to show that an organization actually contributed to the realization of the project.

Because financing tests can be very complex, a positive list of approved financial test parameters (duration, size, etc) is very important to provide a set of easily implementable tests that an organization can use to assess whether their project qualifies. A positive list reduces complexity for organizations when assessing projects.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text: Feasibility is an essential consideration when selecting which additionality tests should be required. Overly onerous additionality requirements would sacrifice implementability and climate action by organizations in pursuit of perfect certainty in reduction claims. If the additionality requirements are too lax, too many low-quality projects that do not actually reduce emissions will receive emissions-reduction credit. A good set of additionality tests will be standardized, easy to understand, and highly implementable to enable organizations to easily assess and procure projects while allowing a minimum of low merit claims to qualify.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text:
Statistical operating margin methodologies based on actual empirical data are a very established field that has shown high alignment between dozens of published studies such as Siler-Evans et al (2012), Zivin et al (2014), Hittinger and Azevedo (2015), Callaway et al (2015), Kotchen et al (2022), and many others.

Koebrich et al. established a series of empirical tests and applied them to seven different marginal emissions models to evaluate how well they align with measurable real-world grid behaviors. They found that models using statistical regression methods performed the best, but that several other models also performed well in certain situations. They found that models based on scenario modeling tend to violate the tests more often, but could still provide value in identifying the best location for new load or generation.

Elenes et al. used a scenario model to compare emission factor methodologies and also found that both locational SCED and statistical methods were accurate in estimating the empirical marginal operating emissions rate. Steinsultz et al. used causal analysis on generation data in ERCOT to estimate the true marginal emissions factor and compared it to several existing models. They found that both statistical and locational SCED models were accurate at estimating the true operating margin. Both statistical and locational SCED models have a history of use in scientific research to estimate marginal emissions impacts and represent the highest-quality marginal emissions factors derived from empirical observations.

Steinsultz et al. also found that heat rate and LMP signals were effective at identifying times of very low marginal operating emissions (due to wind curtailment), but that they did not accurately predict the operating margin rate at higher values. The rank ordering was consistent, but the values were not strongly correlated. These signals may be appropriate in some regions where the marginal fuel is either gas or renewables (such as CAISO or NYISO), but they do not provide meaningful estimates if there are more than one fossil fuel type on the grid.

Importantly, the signals studied were all locational, with geographic resolution smaller than the entire ERCOT region. The operating marginal emissions diverged substantially in different locations at the same time because of the important influence of transmission constraints on curtailment. Therefore, any methodology that uses a single value for a large grid region (such as SCED – fuel on the margin) is not appropriate, since different generators can be marginal simultaneously in different parts of the grid.

Scenario modeling methods are useful for research into the outcomes of different scenarios, but are not appropriate for accounting for real-world actions, because they require significant simplification and assumptions about real-world conditions. The results will not necessarily align with real-world behavior unless significant effort is put into calibrating the scenario against empirical data.

Difference-based models have the property that during times when the denominator is small, they can generate large negative numbers based on small measurement errors.

Resources:
Siler-Evans et al (2012): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22486733/
Zivin et al (2014): https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167268114000808
Hittinger and Azevedo (2015): https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/es505027p
Callaway et al (2015): https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/694179
Kotchen et al (2022): https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.2116632119
Koebrich et al 2025: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1364032125001819?ref=pdf_download&fr=RR-2&rr=9c5b38101d7255c2
Elenes et al 2022: https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/acs.est.2c02344
Steinsultz et al 2024: https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2753-3751/ad72f6/pdf

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text:
Christian et al, 2025 finds substantial agreement between actual historically observed U.S. capacity growth and projections generated from models based on recent capacity additions and capacity expansion modeling. The authors show that these models are able to reproduce the mix of new generation actually built after 2022 in CISO, ERCO, ISNE, MISO, NYIS, PJM, SOCO, and SWPP when supplied only with information available in 2022 (see Figures 1 and 4-9 in the aforementioned paper).

They further compare these models against empirical emissions rates derived from a causal inference natural experiment using multi-year load variation. Models that combine the operating margin and the build margin derived from recent capacity additions (with a build margin weight of ½) exhibit strong agreement with the natural experiment estimates of the actual emissions rates (see Figure 2 in the paper). The capacity expansion model Cambium also shows strong agreement. In contrast, an average emissions rate shows poor agreement, indicating that it fails to capture the long-run behavior reflected in the empirical estimates.

Resources:
Christian et al.: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5425615

answers.label: Assessing model applicability to project types
answers.text:
One factor to consider is that most institutional behavior is typically driven by multiple different interventions that would be very challenging to isolate. For example, if a given building consumes 100 kW in a given hour, that is simultaneously driven by business decisions to consume power; energy efficiency decisions about multiple different pieces of equipment; unrelated appliance cost decisions; energy conservation measures; demand response and load-shaping measures; and other factors. Thus, in practice it’s important to have systems that can measure the sum of many interventions and reach the same conclusion. This suggests that standardization is important.

In theory, the build margin can vary across project parameters and local grid conditions. Models based on recent capacity additions or capacity expansions attempt to account for these variations, but they may still fall short of fully reflecting real-world heterogeneity. In reality, the emissions produced by electricity generation can scale nonlinearly, and different project sizes might require different emissions rates. In practice, this is not feasible and the best practical approach relies on well-constructed averages (e.g., across all recent renewable energy projects). The gold standard in assessing these models are post-hoc analyses on the effect that building the projects had on measured emissions, perhaps to be done annually, but such analyses do not yet exist in the literature. Furthermore, allowing different parameters for different projects encourages gaming to make project investment look better.

Given this current limitation, all models based on such averaged build-margin estimates should be applied broadly across project types and sizes, recognizing that while they cannot capture project-specific parameters, they still provide the most practical approach currently available.

answers.label: Other appropriate emission rates or metrics
answers.text:
For an emissions rate to be validly used to assess the emissions impacts of projects, it must capture the consequential impact of the project, meaning the change in emissions that occurs specifically because of the project rather than due to unrelated factors.

There are fundamentally only two ways to do this. The first is to do a custom consequential analysis of an individual intervention, where the impact is the net difference in total emissions of a scenario that includes an intervention, versus the baseline that does not. Capacity expansion models, when properly paired with dispatch models, can do this.

The second way is to use a standardized estimate of those two values across multiple possible interventions, and divide by the number of megawatt-hours to get the net difference in total emissions per megawatt-hour, generating an emissions rate. Any method that does this inherently is a marginal emissions rate, regardless of whether it was generated statistically or by other means.

In contrast, average emissions rates, for example, are not measures of consequential impact and fail to capture this effect (see, e.g., Elenes et al., 2022; Kotchen et al., 2022; Schram et al., 2019; Siler-Evans et al., 2012).

Resources:
Elenes et al.: https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/acs.est.2c02344
Kotchen et al.: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2116632119
Schram et al.: https://www.scitepress.org/Papers/2019/77657/77657.pdf
Siler-Evans et al.: https://watttime.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Marginal-Emissions-Factors-for-the-US-Electricity-System_April-2012.pdf

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text:
Unlike with attributional, with measured consequential analysis there is no theoretically such thing as maximum granularity. Rather, the only question is at what level of granularity the answers are all the same, or may become unreliable.

The best available research on this topic suggests that, for grids that dispatch on a nodal basis, that occurs at the node. Intra-regional transmission constraints can cause significant variations in marginal emissions rates within even a single zone. Fell et al. demonstrated the link between intra-regional transmission and emissions rates, while Sofia and Dvorkin found that the net emissions impact of hourly and annual electricity matching varied significantly with location in ERCOT and PJM. Similarly, Steinsultz et al. also found that models which predict different marginal emissions rates at different nodes can correctly predict real-world behavior changes in emissions based on this information.

A related practical consideration is that transmission constraints are dynamic over time, making it difficult to create static groups of nodes into zones where there are never any transmission constraints. Thus, where sufficiently accurate data are accessible, it is better to use nodal data if practical.

While nodal granularity offers the best estimate of marginal emissions, less granular spatial resolution may be appropriate based on data availability. The most granular data available should always be used when it meets minimum quality criteria. It also would be unwise to mandate that everyone must always use nodal data, as not all power grids worldwide even have nodes.

Resources:
Fell et al: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/pol.20190258
Sofia ad Dvorkin: https://resurety.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Carbon-Impact-of-Transmission-Constraints.pdf
Steinsultz: https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2753-3751/ad72f6/pdf

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text:
Most power grids worldwide dispatch sub-hourly. One of the biggest single sources of variation in consequential emission factors for electricity is periods of renewable energy curtailment, which frequently last as little as five minutes. Producing renewable energy at this time typically causes no consequential impact at all, and it is critical for both short-run and long-run emissions impact to shift generation away from such times and load to such times. Curtailment is also becoming more common at an exponential rate, and will grow ever more important each year. Thus, we strongly recommend that sub-hourly marginal emissions rates be permissible for those organizations willing and able to do so.

Because renewable energy has strong intra-day variation and diurnal patterns, marginal emissions rates should ideally have at least hourly resolution at minimum to capture those important timing effects.

If even hourly data is not feasible, we recommend institutions use monthly or annual averaged marginal emissions rates weighted by different generation or load profiles. For example, using a typical or expected solar or wind generation profile applied over the course of a year to provide an estimate of the annual average marginal emissions impact of solar or wind generation, because these two technologies will likely have very different impacts because of timing differences. There would then be multiple annual averaged marginal emissions factors to potentially apply and one would be chosen based on the expected hourly profile of the generation or load being added. A single annual averaged marginal emissions factor would not be appropriate to apply to all projects.

answers.label: Appropriate margin weighting approaches
selections: Default 0.50 build margin weight for all projects

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are appropriate
answers.text:
It is easy for theoretical models to speculate on weights, but as far as we are aware, only one empirical study has ever looked at how different build margin weights successfully predicted actual changes in emissions in reality.

Christian et al, 2025 examined a natural experiment in the balancing authorities CISO, ERCO, ISNE, MISO, NYIS, PJM, SOCO and SWPP to empirically compare the actual changes in emissions in these regions with those predicted by various build margin weights. . They found substantial agreement between actual historical changes in emissions and those predicted by empirically determined marginal emissions rates using a build margin weight of ½ (see Figure 2 in the paper). The analysis also showed that a build margin weight of ½ was markedly more consistent with actual historical changes in emissions than a build margin weight of either 0 or 1 (see Figure 3 in the paper).

Resources:
Christian et. al.: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5425615

answers.label: Weighting approaches not feasible to implement
selections: GHG Protocol Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Reductions from Grid-connected Electricity Projects

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are infeasible
answers.text:
WattTime previously assumed that the above options were the most appropriate. After all, in theory, different electricity projects might influence emissions through different proportions of build or operating margins. Consequently, a flexible framework that allows customized weightings between operating and build margin impacts could, in principle, measure consequential emissions more accurately.

However, such flexibility introduces the risk of gameability. A system with too many adjustable parameters, especially if these parameters cannot be standardized rigorously, could enable electricity consumers to strategically manipulate how their projects are classified in order to maximize credited impact.

To explore this, WattTime used scenario modeling to game out how firms that wished to claim as much “credit” as possible would respond to each of the above options. WattTime was surprised to discover that the most common systems to assign variable build margin weight based on the intervention led to a very challenging unintended outcome. Specifically, because build margins are usually systematically lower than operating margins, variable weights incentivize firms to take actions that maximize the build margin weight for clean generation, and minimize it for load.

The problem is that this typically incentivizes firms to deliberately minimize the availability of clean energy and batteries at the moments when they are most critical to grid resource adequacy. In other words, variable build weights incentivize firms to *maximize* grid stress. In practice, this would slow renewables integration and increase long-run emissions.

The GHG Protocol Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Reductions from Grid-connected Electricity Projects suggests that when other measures are not practical, one should use a build margin weight of 0.5. This is why WattTime endorsed this fixed weight.

Future research might allow for a more customized weighting approach, but it would be important to ensure that it does not incentivize firms to maximize emissions.

answers.label: Other approaches for assigning margin weights
answers.text: Any weighting approach has to balance three often competing considerations: the risk of gameability, practical feasibility, and potential emissions-reduction benefits. While it is possible that a weighting system that could optimize all three could be developed in the future, currently there is insufficient research or empirical evidence to identify such a methodology. However, there is sufficient evidence to advise against a weight of 0, of 1, or of a variable weight that incentivizes firms to maximize grid stress.
